About: Moment of Inertia — Where the Mass Sits

Source

Topic
Rotational mechanics — moment of inertia of a point-mass distribution
Concept
For a fixed applied torque, angular acceleration depends far more strongly on where the mass sits than on how much of it there is: I = Σmr², so α = τ/I scales as 1/r².
Audience
JEE (NCERT Class 11-12) — SI units, standard notation.
Serves
Building the intuition that distance-from-axis dominates rotational inertia; distinguishing mass (translational inertia) from moment of inertia (rotational inertia).
Misconception
“A heavier object is harder to spin, so mass is what matters.” Encoded as one of the choices in the prediction step.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A light rod is pivoted at its centre with two identical 0.5 kg masses clamped at d = 0.2 m from the axis. Press Play — a steady torque of 0.4 N·m spins the rod up. Note how briskly it accelerates: α ≈ 10 rad/s².

The applied torque arrow (pink) stays the same size for every setting. Only where the mass sits will change.

2 · Predict

You are about to slide the masses out from 0.2 m to 0.4 m — twice as far from the axis. The mass is unchanged and the torque is unchanged. What happens to the angular acceleration α?

3 · Verify

Now drag the distance slider from 0.2 m out to 0.4 m and watch the rod spin up alongside its ghost. The current run visibly falls behind: α is four times smaller, so angle accumulates far more slowly during spin-up.

The ghost keeps the previous setting so you can compare rates directly, not from memory. Display ω is capped at 8 rad/s — compare during spin-up, before both rods share that cap.

4 · Compare with mass

Return the distance to 0.2 m. Now double the mass instead — slide each mass from 0.5 kg to 1.0 kg. What do you predict for α?

5 · The rule

For point masses, I = Σ mr². With two identical masses on a rod, I = 2mr². Newton's rotational law α = τ/I then makes distance the star: doubling r → ¼× α; doubling m → ½× α.

Now play freely: try light masses far out versus heavy masses close in. Two 0.5 kg at 0.4 m vs. two 1.0 kg at 0.2 m — same total mass, but I differs by a factor of two.

The Physics

Moment of Inertia — Where the Mass Sits · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A light rod, pivoted at its centre, carries two identical masses. A steady torque spins it up from rest. You move the masses along the rod or change their size, and the sim reports how the spin-up responds.

What you'll learn

  • What moment of inertia I measures, and how a torque and I set the angular acceleration.
  • How I depends on the masses and on where they sit relative to the axis.
  • What the radius of gyration k means.
Two masses m sit a distance d from the axis. The torque τ stays the same.

What's on screen

  • Rod and masses: the blue rod spins about the axis at its centre. A dashed line marks d to the right-hand mass.
  • Ghost rod (grey, dashed): the setting you had just before your last slider change, spinning up for comparison.
  • Torque arrow (pink): a curved arrow of fixed size, labelled with τ.
  • ω label below the ring, and the Live quantities panel with I, α and k.
See itSpin the rod up with the opening settings. Watch for: the rod speeding up from rest, with the ω label at the bottom rising to its limit of 8 rad/s.

03

A torque produces angular acceleration α = τ/I

A net force gives a body a linear acceleration, a = F/m. A net torque gives it an angular acceleration, and the mass is replaced by the moment of inertia I:

α = τ / I
τ in N·m, I in kg·m², α in rad/s².

I measures how hard a body is to set spinning about a given axis. It is not a property of the body alone: it depends on the axis chosen, and on both how much mass there is and where that mass sits.

  • At fixed I, doubling τ doubles α.
  • At fixed τ, a larger I gives a smaller α.
See itDouble the torque to 0.80 N·m, with the d = 0.20 m, m = 0.50 kg ghost for comparison. Watch for: I staying at 0.0400 kg·m² while α rises from 10.00 to 20.00 rad/s², and the blue rod pulling ahead of the grey ghost.
04

Each mass adds m r² to I, so distance counts twice

For point masses, each one adds its mass times the square of its distance from the axis. With two identical masses at distance d on a light rod:

I = Σ mi ri² = 2 m d²
Linear in m, quadratic in d.

So doubling d multiplies I by 2² = 4, and with τ fixed, α falls to a quarter. At m = 0.50 kg and τ = 0.40 N·m:

dIα
0.20 m0.0400 kg·m²10.00 rad/s²
0.40 m0.1600 kg·m²2.50 rad/s²

Mass far from the axis has to move faster for the same ω, so it resists being spun up more.

See itMove the masses out to d = 0.40 m. Watch for: the grey ghost rod (d = 0.20 m) spinning up faster than the blue rod, and α reading 2.50 rad/s².
05

Doubling the mass only doubles I

In I = 2md², the mass enters once and the distance enters twice. Doubling m at fixed d doubles I and halves α. Doubling d at fixed m quadruples I.

Total mass alone therefore does not settle how hard the rod is to spin. Where it sits matters more:

  • Two 0.50 kg masses at d = 0.40 m give I = 0.16 kg·m².
  • Two 1.00 kg masses at d = 0.20 m give I = 0.08 kg·m², half as much, although the masses are heavier.

Same torque, so the second rod has twice the α: 5.00 against 2.50 rad/s².

See itCompare 0.50 kg at d = 0.40 m (blue) with 1.00 kg at d = 0.20 m (grey ghost). Watch for: the heavier, closer ghost rod spinning up faster than the blue rod, and α reading 2.50 rad/s² for the blue one.
06

The radius of gyration k gives I = Mk²

The radius of gyration k is the distance at which the whole mass M could be placed to give the same moment of inertia about the same axis:

I = M k², k = √(I / M)
Here M = 2m is the total of the two masses.

Both masses sit at distance d, so I = 2md² = (2m)d², and k = d exactly. The k readout therefore follows the distance slider. For a spread-out body k lies between the nearest and the farthest part of the mass.

See itSet d = 0.35 m. Watch for: the k readout showing 0.35 m, the same as d.
07

Where it matters

  • Flywheels. A flywheel puts its mass in a heavy rim. For a given mass this gives a large I, so it resists changes in its spin.
  • Balancing poles. A tightrope walker's long pole puts mass far from the body's axis. The large I makes the body turn slowly, which gives time to correct a tilt.
  • Gymnasts and divers. Tucking the limbs in brings mass closer to the axis, lowers I and makes a somersault faster.
  • Choosing the axis. The same body has a different I about a different axis. That is why a problem always names the axis.
08

Summary

In one line. A torque spins a body up at α = τ/I, and the moment of inertia I depends on how the mass is arranged about the axis, not only on how much there is.

Key points

  • α = τ/I is Newton's second law for rotation.
  • For point masses I = Σmr²; here I = 2md².
  • k = √(I/M) is the distance that would give the same I with all the mass at one radius.

Common mix-ups

  • "A heavier body is always harder to spin." Not by itself. Mass close to the axis adds little to I, and mass far from it adds a lot.
  • "I is a number that belongs to the body." It belongs to the body and the axis together. Change the axis and I changes.
  • "The torque got bigger because the masses moved out." The applied τ stayed the same. It is I that changed, and with it α.

Things to try on your own

  • Keep τ = 0.40 N·m and find the d that gives α = 5 rad/s² with m = 0.50 kg, then check I and k.
  • Find a pair of m and d with the same I as the opening setting but a different d.
  • Predict I and α for m = 2.00 kg and d = 0.50 m at τ = 1.00 N·m, then test it.
